standard.title: Sounds and rhythms of the target language
standard.description: recognise and imitate the sounds and rhythms of the target language
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have noticed target language sounds and imitated some with support (AC9LSF02). They have no prior systematic experience with target language phonology, vowel patterns or the full sound inventory.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise and imitate the sounds and rhythms of the target language — including vowel patterns, consonant features, intonation and sounds not present in English.

nodes.label: Target language sounds and alphabet features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise and imitate distinctive sounds of the target language, including sounds not present in English, and apply correct sound patterns to familiar vocabulary.
nodes.minimum_width: Correctly produce target language vowel patterns in familiar words; imitate at least two target language sounds not present in English with adequate accuracy.
nodes.typical_width: Apply correct vowel patterns across known vocabulary; imitate distinctive consonant features; recognise silent letters and other sound conventions; differentiate sounds that are similar but distinct in the target language; participate in alphabet songs and games that embed sound-letter relationships.
wider: Explain the difference between at least two target language sounds and their nearest English approximations — demonstrating metalinguistic awareness
Compare target language and English sound conventions for common concepts (e.g. animal sounds, exclamations) — identify where conventions differ
nodes.hinge_reason: Accurate target language sound patterns are the phonological foundation for all subsequent pronunciation and literacy work. Students who default to English sound patterns produce persistent errors that are increasingly difficult to remediate at higher bands.

response_modes.reason: Sound pattern production requires repeated practice until new sound conventions become automatic. Songs, chants and games embed high-frequency practice in engaging contexts.

success_criteria: Produces target language vowel patterns accurately in familiar words
Imitates at least two target language sounds not present in English with adequate accuracy for recognition

nodes.label: Intonation, rhythm and statement/question distinction
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can recognise and imitate target language intonation patterns — including the distinction between statements and questions — and produce spoken language with appropriate rhythm and pace.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate the difference between statement and question intonation in at least one example pair; produce a short sentence with appropriate rhythm.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise and use intonation to distinguish statements from questions and exclamations; develop phrasing and rhythm through songs, chants and movement; notice and imitate sound patterns; apply appropriate pace and stress in familiar spoken texts.
wider: Perform a familiar chant or song with deliberate attention to rhythm, stress and pace — demonstrating prosodic control beyond word-level accuracy
Produce the same sentence as a statement and a question — demonstrating intonation distinction — and explain what changes

response_modes.reason: Prosodic awareness develops through varied experience with the rhythmic and melodic patterns of the language. Songs, rhymes and chants across different moods and speeds build the range of intonation patterns students need.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Prosodic control — rhythm, intonation, pace — is what makes spoken target language sound natural rather than recited. Width investment here builds the musicality of language that underpins genuine oral fluency.
success_criteria: Demonstrates different intonation for at least one statement-question pair
Produces a short familiar spoken text with appropriate rhythm and pace
